kernels.verified_summary:
On the 32 matrices (31 dev-size and square47, one H200, 50 repetitions, all checks passed) the timings decide two things and price a third. All numbers below were recomputed from sweeps/*.json; the analyst's tables are numerically correct.

Decided by the data: scheduling. For rows, length-binned lane groups up to 64 entries (B) take 0.69x of one thread per row up to 64 (H), 0.19x of cuOpt's one block per row (C) and 0.10x of one thread per row (T) in geomean with compensated sums; T is 371x slower on bab6 (80.7 ms against 0.217 ms). C costs about 9 ns per row in plain and 20.5 ns in compensated arithmetic: 10x / 17x slower than B on the 16 matrices with mean row length up to 16, 1.7x / 2.5x on the 7 between 16 and 64, and from 0.77x to 2.58x on the 9 above 64 (faster on sp98ar, supportcase19, supportcase7, trento1; 2.6x slower on square47, whose mean is 444 but 96% of whose rows have at most 2 entries). For columns the answer depends on size: below 1e6 nonzeros B takes 2.00 ms against 4.21 ms for H in total (21 matrices, B up to 5.9x faster), from 1e6 to 1e7 H takes 3.03 ms against 3.87 ms (H faster on 7 of 10, up to 1.94x, 354 us on kasavu). As one fixed combination B/S/A/comp + B/S/comp/gated is 1.094x the per-matrix best in geomean, but that is 1.01 to 1.04 in bands A1 to B1 and 1.195 in B2, 1.330 in B3 (worst 1.63 kasavu). The in-sample rule 'H for columns when the model has at least 1e5 columns' gives 1.042 overall (B2 1.021, B3 1.133); the data cannot place its threshold between 40,623 and 114,240 columns.

Also decided: rebuild. The stable radix sort (467 us + 0.279 ns per original nonzero) beats scatter + segmented sort on 24 of 32 totals (1.45x geomean, 5.1x on rd-rplusc-21) and loses 7% and 9% on supportcase6 and bab6; compacting the old CSC takes 0.70x of it on all 32 but only works for deletions; one CPU thread is faster on 4 of the 6 matrices up to 100,933 nonzeros (1.79x on istanbul-no-cutoff).

Priced: compensated sums cost 39% in the B activity kernel (1.08x to 2.02x), nothing measurable in the candidate kernel, 14% on the round: medians of 5 us in bands A1 and A2, 173 us in B3, 371 us on square47.

Not decided by time: layout, count method under B, and gating. Two variants that do identical work at run time (H with A against H with R on the four matrices without a row above 64 entries) differ by up to 12% in plain and 3% in comp, and pass the report's 3%-and-spread test in 4 of 8 plain pairs; the compensated candidate kernel is 'faster' than the plain one on 19 matrices. Inside that band: S against P with atomic counts (0.992 / 0.993 activity; candidates 1.027 plain, 0.998 comp like for like), A against R under B/S (0.971 plain, 1.000 comp), gated against always (0.991). Outside it: in cuOpt's scheme the atomic count against the second cub::BlockReduce pair is 0.706 (plain, 32 of 32) and 0.842 (comp), and that is the whole gain; split arrays add nothing once the count reduction is gone (C/S/A against C/P/A 0.9965 / 0.9992). So the PR 2372 review's 'no extra block reduction for counts' is supported for block reductions (still 12% plain, 2% comp with integer counts), and 'split arrays' is neither supported nor opposed by time. A loses 8.5% to 10.7% only on supportcase42, the one matrix where 94% of the rows hold two or more infinite terms; matrices where nearly every row holds exactly one (rmatr200-p5, rd-rplusc-21) show no loss.

Round cost for the work estimate: the fastest measured round is 61 us (radiationm18-12-05), band A1 median 95 us; fits give 81 to 89 us + 0.14 ns per nonzero (relative) or 165 to 225 us + 0.11 (least squares), so both the constant and the slope (0.11 to 0.23 for the fixed combination) depend on the fit; single matrices are 0.5x (neos-4647030-tutaki) to 3.1x (neos-4306827-ravan) off.

Not in the analyst's report: the benchmark's frontier-restricted activity sweep (compaction + H/S/A) is slower than a full B sweep of all rows on all 16 matrices below 5e5 nonzeros at every frontier size down to 0.01% of the rows, because compaction alone costs 34 to 67 us; from 1e6 nonzeros it wins at frontiers of 1% of the rows and below. And B changes the summation order that DESIGN.md 2.4 describes (H): its sums differ in bits from the one-thread order on 9 of 32 matrices (H on 5), so B for full sweeps next to an H frontier kernel gives two orders for one row.

Not measured and able to change the picture: a state stored in binned order (B and H pay a scattered write here), re-binning at a rebuild, a frontier-restricted B or candidate kernel, lane groups with more than two entries per lane, other bin boundaries than 64 and 8192, the error guard, sweeps after tightening, a second GPU type, and sizes above 1e7 nonzeros beyond square47.

verified_recommendations.decision: Activity layout
verified_recommendations.value: Split arrays (S), as DESIGN.md 2.4 already states. The timings do not decide it; they show that it costs nothing in the recommended kernel.
verified_recommendations.evidence: With atomic counts S / P is 0.992 (plain) and 0.993 (comp) in the B activity kernel, 30 and 30 of 32 within 3%, no matrix with P faster outside the spread. Candidate kernel, like for like (S always against P, both load lo): 0.998 for B, 30 of 32 within 3%. Whole compensated B round: regret 1.094 with S, 1.104 with P. In cuOpt's scheme with reduced counts S is 0.796 (plain, 30 of 32) and 0.861 (comp, 31 of 32), but only because the paired layout reduces the counts as doubles: with atomic counts C/S against C/P is 0.9965 and 0.9992.
verified_recommendations.uncertainty: All of the S-against-P differences under B lie inside the band in which two variants doing identical work differ (up to 12% plain, 3% comp), so 'S is 1% faster' is not a finding. S loses in the plain candidate kernel on 10 matrices, at most 10.1% (istanbul-no-cutoff), geomean 2.7%, and 3.2% on istanbul-no-cutoff with comp gated. What S buys in the design (bytes per row, a cold lo array, the flag bit that allows gating) is not measured here. PR 2372's request for split arrays is neither supported nor opposed by these timings.

verified_recommendations.decision: Count method
verified_recommendations.value: No second block reduction for counts: scan and one integer atomic (A) in the block and chunk kernels. In the lane-group kernel the timings do not separate A from R.
verified_recommendations.evidence: Where R is a second cub::BlockReduce pair: C/P A / R 0.706 plain (A faster on 32 of 32) and 0.842 comp (31 of 32); C/S 0.883 and 0.977; B/S on the 6 matrices with at most 1% of nonzeros in rows up to 64: 0.938 plain (0.894 to 0.990), 0.990 comp. In the lane-group kernel (7 matrices with at least 99% of nonzeros in rows up to 64): 1.016 in both arithmetics. Over all 32 under B/S: 0.971 plain, 1.000 comp. The review's 'no extra block reduction for counts' is supported for block reductions.
verified_recommendations.uncertainty: In the recommended arithmetic the choice does not change the round time as measured (1.000). A loses 10.7% (plain) and 8.5% (comp) on supportcase42, the only matrix where 94% of the rows hold two or more infinite terms; matrices with one infinite term in nearly every row (rmatr200-p5, rd-rplusc-21) show no loss. Carrying the count through the shuffles in the lane-group kernel and using the atomic only in block kernels would avoid that loss, but this mixed kernel was not timed. Bounds are the original ones; after tightening fewer terms are infinite. Differences below about 10% in plain between two template instances can be code generation (null comparison: 0.876 to 1.012 for identical work).

verified_recommendations.decision: Row scheduling for a full sweep
verified_recommendations.value: B: rows binned by length, lane groups up to 64 entries, one 256-thread block per row from 65 to 8192, chunks above. Never T, and not C, as the general scheme.
verified_recommendations.evidence: Layout S, counts A, comp: B takes 0.69x of H (faster on 23, slower on 5), 0.19x of C (faster on 26, slower on 4), 0.10x of T (faster on 27, slower on 5) in geomean; total over the 32 matrices 6.29 ms for B, 7.79 ms for H, 67.5 ms for C, 294 ms for T. B is the row scheduling of the best timed compensated round on 19 of 32 matrices. T is 371x slower on bab6. C costs about 9 ns (plain) and 20.5 ns (comp) per row: 10x / 17x slower than B on the 16 matrices with mean row length up to 16. A row rule between B and H cannot gain more than 1.094 to 1.084 in round regret.
verified_recommendations.uncertainty: B loses to H on kasavu 1.16x, kenana 1.15x, supportcase42 1.15x, rd-rplusc-21 1.12x (1.37x in plain), rmatr200-p5 1.12x; to C on sp98ar 1.30x, supportcase19 1.27x, supportcase7 1.18x, trento1 1.10x; to T on kasavu 1.38x, cygnet 1.31x, supportcase42 1.30x, kenana 1.23x, sorrell3 1.06x (comp). In band B3 B is not the fastest row scheme on 4 of 5 matrices. B is not the scheme DESIGN.md 2.4 describes (that is H): its sums follow a lane tree and differ in bits from the one-thread order on 9 of 32 matrices (H on 5; hi + lo as a double is equal on all 32), and the only frontier kernel measured is H, so adopting B needs either a frontier B kernel or the decision that two summation orders for one row are acceptable. B and H were timed with a second sorted copy of the CSR and a scattered write through a row map; storage in binned order and re-binning at a rebuild are not measured. Bin boundaries 64 and 8192 were not varied; with compensated sums one thread per row beats one block per row at 128 entries on cygnet (0.670 ms against 0.877 ms).

verified_recommendations.decision: Column scheduling for the candidate kernel
verified_recommendations.value: B below 1e6 nonzeros. Above that the measured default is wrong on most matrices: use H (one thread per column up to 64) for models with many columns, with the switch point to be fixed on more data (in-sample candidate: at least 1e5 columns).
verified_recommendations.evidence: S, comp gated. Below 1e6 nonzeros (21 matrices): B 2.00 ms against H 4.21 ms in total; B faster by up to 5.9x (ns1208400) and 320 us (istanbul-no-cutoff). From 1e6 to 1e7 (10 matrices): H 3.03 ms against B 3.87 ms; H faster on 7. B loses on 8 matrices, all with at least 114,240 columns: kasavu 1.94x (354 us), kenana 1.93x, supportcase7 1.71x, bab6 1.67x, savsched1 1.61x, supportcase19 1.61x, supportcase6 1.47x, supportcase12 1.15x. Round regret with always B: 1.094 overall, 1.195 in band B2, 1.330 in B3; with 'H when cols >= 1e5': 1.042 overall, 1.021 in B2, 1.133 in B3; bound of any column rule 1.037.
verified_recommendations.uncertainty: The rule is read off the same 32 matrices. No matrix has between 40,623 and 95,030 columns, and any threshold from 40,624 to 114,240 scores 1.042 to 1.044, so the data do not place it. Columns may not be the right variable: square47 (95,030 columns) prefers B by 1.106x (256 us) and neos-4306827-ravan (162,291 columns, 26 long columns) by 1.18x; H loses 1.9x on neos-4647030-tutaki and 1.46x on cygnet among the large matrices. Needs the 8 large testbed instances without a sweep file and the held-out set. Lane groups with more than two entries per lane, which could remove the need for a rule, were not measured. No frontier-restricted candidate kernel exists in the benchmark.

verified_recommendations.decision: Arithmetic
verified_recommendations.value: Compensated (hi, lo) sums in both kernels, lo loaded in the candidate kernel only when the flag bit says it is nonzero (gated). The timings give the price; they do not show the benefit.
verified_recommendations.evidence: Activity B/S/A comp / plain 1.386 (1.083 radiationm18-12-05 to 2.024 cygnet; plain faster on 32 of 32); extra time 0.007 to 0.37 ns per nonzero, median 0.052. Candidate kernel B/S: no measurable cost (0.972, which cannot be an effect of the arithmetic). Whole round 1.143 (0.984 to 1.514): medians of 5.5 us in A1, 5.0 in A2, 13.7 in A3, 36 in B1, 79 in B2, 173 in B3, 371 us on square47. Gated / always: 0.991 for B (31 of 32 within 3%; sorrell3 0.884), 0.9955 for H; no matrix with 'always' faster outside the spread for B.
verified_recommendations.uncertainty: The value of compensation lies in incremental updates, which the benchmark does not run; on one fresh full sweep compensated and plain candidate bounds differ on 5 of 32 matrices by at most 2.2e-9. The cost is highest where rows go through the block kernel: cygnet 2.02x, splice1k1 1.89x, triptim1 1.72x. The gating gain of 0.9% in geomean is inside the null band; gating costs 0.9% to 2.7% on the 4 matrices with more than 10% nonzero-lo rows (rd-rplusc-21 2.7%). The design's error guard, which would skip more lo loads, is not modelled. The benchmark's plain and compensated candidate variants are timed in a fixed order, and differences of up to 10% between them (supportcase19) are unexplained.

verified_recommendations.decision: Rebuild method
verified_recommendations.value: Compact the CSR, then build the CSC with the stable radix sort on (column, position); when the rebuild is deletions only, compact the old CSC instead.
verified_recommendations.evidence: Radix total 467 us + 0.279 ns per original nonzero (relative fit, median error 4.9%, 0.85x to 1.53x). Against scatter + segmented sort it is faster on 24 of 32 totals (geomean 1.45x; rd-rplusc-21 5.1x, cygnet 4.9x, square47 3.4x); the segmented sort degrades with the share of nonzeros in columns above 64 entries (Spearman 0.87). Compaction of the old CSC takes 0.70x of the radix total on all 32 (343 us + 0.170 ns per nonzero). The unordered scatter is 0.72x of the radix CSC step but its entry order depends on thread timing, which DESIGN.md 2.5 excludes.
verified_recommendations.uncertainty: Radix loses to the segmented sort on bab6 (9%) and supportcase6 (7%). One CPU thread is faster than the radix total on istanbul-no-cutoff 1.79x, ns1208400 1.44x, wachplan 1.44x, ns1830653 1.29x (all at or below 100,933 nonzeros) and than the old-CSC compaction on istanbul-no-cutoff 1.30x and ns1208400 1.06x; the crossing is around 1e5 nonzeros, at the lower edge of the measured range, and moves with the row and column count (GPU faster on radiationm18-12-05 at 96,149). The CPU figure does not include moving a device-resident matrix to the host and back. Measured with 20% of rows and columns removed in independent draws only; re-binning by length, which scheme B needs after a rebuild, is not timed. One matrix above 1e7 nonzeros; limit 2^31 - 1 nonzeros.

verified_recommendations.decision: Frontier restriction of the GPU activity sweep (added; not in the analyst's list)
verified_recommendations.value: Below about 5e5 nonzeros recompute all rows with the full B sweep; use the compaction-based frontier path only from about 1e6 nonzeros and for frontiers of about 1% of the rows or less.
verified_recommendations.evidence: results.frontier against the full B/S/A sweep of the same arithmetic. Below 5e5 nonzeros (16 matrices) the frontier path (compaction + H/S/A) is slower at every frontier size: plain 16 of 16 at 10%, 1%, 0.1% and 0.01% of the rows; comp 16, 16, 15, 15; geomean 2.5x at 10% and 1.5x at 0.01%. Compaction alone is 33.6 to 66.6 us (median 50.2), above the whole B sweep on the smallest matrices (29.0 us on istanbul-no-cutoff). From 1e6 nonzeros (11 matrices) the frontier path is slower on 3 at 10%, 1 at 1% (comp), 0 at 0.1% and 0.01%, geomean 0.58, 0.41, 0.28, 0.25.
verified_recommendations.uncertainty: In-sample size boundaries; 5 matrices between 5e5 and 1e6 are mixed. The frontier is a random share of the rows, the kernel is H only (latency of up to 64 entries per thread), and compaction is two cub::DeviceSelect calls plus one read-back; a flag test inside the full kernel, a frontier B kernel and a frontier candidate kernel were not measured. Whether the host engine is cheaper than either at small frontiers is a separate question (results.cpu).

verified_recommendations.decision: Constants for the work estimate of one full GPU round
verified_recommendations.value: Compensated, recommended fixed combination: about 60 to 95 us at the small end (fastest measured round 61 us, band A1 median 95 us), then about 0.14 ns per nonzero (relative fit 89 us + 0.145; about 6 us less when the two kernels are timed as one unit). Plain: 88 us + 0.108.
verified_recommendations.evidence: Relative fits over 32 matrices from 71,477 to 27,329,856 nonzeros; best combination as timed 81.4 us + 0.136 (comp), 78.7 us + 0.099 (plain). Constant share of the fitted time 86% at 1e5 nonzeros, 37% at 1e6, 5.6% at 1e7. One launch plus synchronise costs 9.0 us and each further launch about 3.2 us (fixed_costs.json), so launches explain at most about 31 us of a round.
verified_recommendations.uncertainty: Both parameters depend on the fit: for the fixed combination the constant is 86 to 225 us and the slope 0.115 to 0.229 ns per nonzero across relative and least-squares fits with and without square47; the fitted constant is above the fastest measured round, so it is not a floor. Median fit error 22% to 26%; single matrices from 0.5x (neos-4647030-tutaki) to 3.1x (neos-4306827-ravan). The per-matrix cost follows structure (rows in block kernels, long columns), not nonzeros alone. Warm numbers on an idle H200 with buffers allocated; kernels that follow a round in a presolve are not included; nothing below 71,477 nonzeros was measured although band A1 starts at 5e4.

claims_found_wrong.claim: A loses 8.5% to 10.7% on supportcase42, 'where every row holds infinite terms and the lane-group kernel does the atomics' (summary, finding on counts, recommendation).
claims_found_wrong.correct: The numbers are right, the stated condition is not what separates supportcase42. Matrices where nearly every row holds exactly one infinite term show no loss: rmatr200-p5 (100.0% / 99.5% of rows, 99.8% of nonzeros in rows up to 64) A / R 0.981 plain, 1.003 comp; rd-rplusc-21 (94.4% / 98.1%) 1.002, 1.017; trento1 (99.8% on the minimum side) 0.986, 1.006. supportcase42 is the only matrix where 94.4% of the rows hold two or more infinite terms on both sides (rows_by_infinite_terms = [0, 1027, 17412]). The data tie the loss of A to rows with two or more infinite terms, not to rows with an infinite term. One matrix, so the mechanism (several lanes of a group adding to the same counter) stays a hypothesis.
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: matrix.rows_by_infinite_terms_min/max and results.activity B/S/A against B/S/R for all 32 matrices; new table in script section 1.3.

claims_found_wrong.claim: Arithmetic recommendation: compensated costs '1.08x to 2.02x; 0.03 to 0.06 ns per nonzero' in the activity kernel.
claims_found_wrong.correct: The extra time of B/S/A/comp over B/S/A/plain is 0.007 ns per nonzero (square47) to 0.37 (trento1), median 0.052. 0.029 and 0.049 are the medians of two groups (7 light-only and 6 block-only matrices), not a range.
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: (ms comp - ms plain) * 1e6 / nnz per matrix from results.activity.

claims_found_wrong.claim: Arithmetic recommendation: 'Gating is worth 1% at most here'.
claims_found_wrong.correct: 1% is the geomean (gated / always 0.991 for B, 0.9955 for H). Single matrices gain more: sorrell3 11.6% (B, 10.5 us, outside the spread), satellites2-60-fs 7.9% (H). On the four matrices with more than 10% nonzero-lo rows gating costs 0.9% to 2.7% (B), all within 3%.
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: results.candidate B/S/comp/gated against B/S/comp/always and the H pair, per matrix.

claims_found_wrong.claim: Layout: 'In the compensated candidate kernel S is 1.1% (B) and 2.0% (H) faster' (summary: 'is 1.1% faster in the compensated candidate kernel').
claims_found_wrong.correct: That is S with a gated lo load against P, which always loads lo (sweeps.cu load_side), so it mixes layout and gating. Like for like (S always against P): 0.998 for B (30 of 32 within 3%, 2 inside the spread, none faster either way) and 0.984 for H (S faster on 6, P on 2). The layout itself gives nothing measurable in the B candidate kernel; the 0.9% is the gating that the flag bit in the uint16 count makes possible.
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: results.candidate B/S/comp/always against B/P/comp (and H); source of load_side.

claims_found_wrong.claim: Summary: C is 'level (1.01x / 1.09x) on the 9 with mean row length above 64'.
claims_found_wrong.correct: 1.01 / 1.09 is a geomean over a spread of 0.79 to 1.92 (plain) and 0.77 to 2.58 (comp). In that group C is slower on square47 1.92x / 2.58x (mean row 444, but 96.3% of its rows have at most 2 entries), neos-4647030-tutaki 1.28x / 1.52x and supportcase6 1.10x / 1.26x, faster on sp98ar, supportcase19, supportcase7, trento1 (0.77 to 0.91 comp), level on splice1k1 and cygnet (0.98 to 0.99, where B and C run the same block kernel on every row). Mean row length does not classify square47.
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: C/S/A against B/S/A per matrix in the group, matrix.row_classes.

claims_found_wrong.claim: Table 1 caption: 'thread entries' = entries one thread of a 256-thread block walks on the longest row / column above 64 entries.
claims_found_wrong.correct: For a matrix with a row or column above 8192 entries the column holds 32 + (mean length of the 65..8192 class) / 256, a lower bound summed over two launches: neos-4306827-ravan 52.8 = 32 + 5328 / 256, square47 46.5 = 32 + 3716 / 256, rd-rplusc-21 36.2. No thread of one block walks more than 32 entries there. The script's docstring states this definition; the report's caption does not.
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: Recomputed from matrix.col_classes / row_classes; script method block_thread_entries.

claims_found_wrong.claim: Off-fit table: neos-5052403-cygnet 1.54 '(activity 2.63x; all 38,268 rows in the block class)'.
claims_found_wrong.correct: The round that was timed on cygnet is T/P/-/comp + B/P/comp: one thread per row over 128 entries, no block kernel. Its activity part (0.670 ms) is 2.63x the activity fit because every row has 128 entries for one thread; the block class explains why B (0.877 ms) is slower still, not the 2.63. The same holds for kenana (T/S/-/comp in the timed round).
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: results.round names for the two matrices; results.activity.

claims_found_wrong.claim: Constants recommendation: 'the constant is known to a factor of two' with one per-nonzero figure (0.14 comp, 0.10 plain).
claims_found_wrong.correct: The slope depends on the fit as much as the constant. For B/S/A/comp + B/S/comp/gated: 0.145 (relative, 32 matrices), 0.156 (relative, without square47), 0.115 (least squares, 32), 0.229 (least squares, without square47) ns per nonzero; constants 89, 86, 225, 99 us. And the fitted constant is not a floor: the fastest measured round is 61.0 us comp / 62.2 us plain (radiationm18-12-05, 96,149 nonzeros), below the 81.4 / 78.7 us constants.
claims_found_wrong.how_checked: Own weighted and unweighted fits; script section 3.4 (existing rows and the new table of fastest rounds).

claims_unsupported.claim: Counts A against R decide anything inside scheduling B: 'A / R 0.971 plain (A faster on 14)', and the H figures 0.884 / 0.925 plain.
claims_unsupported.why: A null comparison in the same files shows the size of differences that are not caused by the count method. In scheme H a row of at most 64 entries is folded by one thread and the count code is never executed (act_light_kernel, class 0); istanbul-no-cutoff, radiationm18-12-05, sorrell3 and supportcase42 have no row above 64, so H/x/A and H/x/R do the same work at run time. Their ratio A / R is 0.876 to 1.012 in plain (istanbul-no-cutoff 0.877 / 0.876, supportcase42 0.931 / 0.926; 4 of 8 pairs pass the 3%-and-spread test) and 0.970 to 0.998 in comp. B/S A / R of 0.971 (plain) and 1.000 (comp), and the H ratios on light rows, lie inside that band. Only the block-kernel effect is outside it: C/P 0.706 / 0.842, and B/S on the two all-block matrices 0.894 / 0.897 plain (0.980 / 0.982 comp).

claims_unsupported.claim: Split layout S 'is never slower' / is 1% faster in the recommended kernel (S / P 0.992, 0.993), used as weak support for S.
claims_unsupported.why: A 1% difference is far inside the null band above (up to 12% plain, 3% comp between variants doing identical work). The timings neither support nor oppose S in the B/A kernel. The only layout effect outside the band is in scheme C with reduced counts (0.796 / 0.861), and it belongs to the double-typed count reduction: with atomic counts C/S against C/P is 0.9965 / 0.9992.

claims_unsupported.claim: Count recommendation: A in the block and chunk kernels, shuffled counts in the lane-group kernel.
claims_unsupported.why: The mixed kernel was not built or timed (the analyst says so). In the recommended arithmetic the block-kernel gain of A is 0.990 on the six block-only matrices and 1.000 over all 32, so the choice does not change the round time as measured; the plain gain (0.938 on those six) is the only timing basis under B.

claims_unsupported.claim: 'The candidate kernel is bound by the entries one thread walks': 2.96 us per entry of a block thread, 3.1 us per entry for H's single thread; ravan 'pays about 0.3 ms for 26 columns'.
claims_unsupported.why: The block-thread term rests on four matrices with at least 16 such entries (supportcase42, ravan, rd-rplusc-21, splice1k1), its regressor is a lower bound built from class means for three of them, and the terms are correlated (the analyst states this for the activity model, not here). With the term the worst residual is still 2.3x. The long columns of ravan are the only visible reason for its 4.8x, but no measurement isolates them: hypothesis, not a kernel constant.

claims_unsupported.claim: The compensated B/S candidate kernel being 2.8% faster than the plain one is caused by run order or code generation (the analyst labels it a hypothesis).
claims_unsupported.why: Stays a hypothesis; the files cannot separate order from code generation. What the files do show: comp does strictly more arithmetic and is 'faster' outside the spread on 19 of 32 matrices (supportcase19 10.3%), so the 3%-and-spread test does not protect candidate comparisons either.

claims_unsupported.claim: 'Break-even near 109,000 nonzeros' between the GPU radix rebuild and one CPU thread.
claims_unsupported.why: It is the crossing of two fitted lines; the CPU line has residuals of 0.45x to 2.2x (3.1x with square47). Measured: CPU faster on 4 of the 6 matrices up to 100,933 nonzeros, level on trento1 (1.02x at 93,571), GPU faster on radiationm18-12-05 (0.72x at 96,149) and supportcase40 (0.95x at 104,420). The data say 'around 1e5, at the lower edge of the measured range, with the row and column count moving it by 30% or more'. The comparison also leaves out what a CPU rebuild of a device-resident matrix needs (download and upload), which is in fixed_costs.json, not here.

claims_unsupported.claim: Column rule 'H when columns >= 1e5'.
claims_unsupported.why: In-sample, as the analyst says. missed_by_analyst: Null band. Two variants that do identical work at run time differ by up to 12.4% in plain and 3% in comp: H/x/A against H/x/R on the 4 matrices without a row above 64 entries gives A / R 0.876 to 1.012 (plain; istanbul-no-cutoff 0.0425 ms against 0.0485 ms) and 0.970 to 0.998 (comp); 4 of 8 plain pairs pass the '3% and outside p10..p90' test. In the candidate kernel comp is 'faster' than plain on 19 of 32 matrices although it does more arithmetic. The 3% threshold with the spread test therefore measures repeatability inside one process, not the effect of a factor. Inside the band and so undecided by time: S against P with atomic counts (0.992 / 0.993), A against R under B/S (0.971 / 1.000), gated against always (0.991), S against P in the candidate kernel (1.027 plain, 0.998 comp like for like).

The regret of the recommended fixed combination sits on the large matrices. B/S/A/comp + B/S/comp/gated by band: A1 1.021, A2 1.010, A3 1.043, B1 1.037, B2 1.195 (max 1.44 supportcase7), B3 1.330 (max 1.63 kasavu), square47 1.000. Sum over the 32: 14.56 ms always B, 13.37 ms with the rule, 12.58 ms for the best combination of each matrix.

Column scheduling by size in absolute time (candidate kernel, S, comp gated): below 1e6 nonzeros (21 matrices) B 2.00 ms against H 4.21 ms in total; 1e6 to 1e7 (10 matrices) B 3.87 ms against H 3.03 ms; square47 B 2.41 against H 2.66. 'B as the default' is the right call below 1e6 and the wrong one on 7 of the 10 matrices of bands B2 and B3.

Frontier path against the full sweep (results.frontier, not used in the report). The benchmark's frontier-restricted activity sweep (two cub::DeviceSelect compactions, one read-back, H/S/A kernels) is slower than the full B/S/A sweep of all rows on all 16 matrices below 5e5 nonzeros at every frontier size down to 0.01% of the rows (plain 16 of 16 at 10%, 1%, 0.1%, 0.01%; comp 16, 16, 15, 15; geomean 2.5x at 10%, 1.5x at 0.01%). Compaction alone costs 33.6 to 66.6 us (median 50.2), more than the whole B sweep on the smallest matrices (istanbul-no-cutoff 29.0 us). From 1e6 nonzeros (11 matrices) the frontier path wins: slower on 3 at 10%, 1 at 1% (comp), 0 at 0.1% and 0.01% (geomean 0.58, 0.41, 0.28, 0.25). Between 5e5 and 1e6 it is mixed (5 matrices). A flag test inside the full kernel was not measured.

Summation order and DESIGN.md 2.4. The design describes scheme H ('each affected row is folded by one thread over its entries in storage order', 'all rows are recomputed with the same kernel'); README_sweeps.md says so. B's lane-group tree is not bitwise equal to the one-thread sum on 9 of 32 matrices, H on 5, so B and H give different bits for rows up to 64 entries on at least ns1208400, neos-4306827-ravan, rd-rplusc-21, supportcase7. With B for full sweeps and the only measured frontier kernel (H), the bits of a row's (hi, lo) depend on which kernel recomputed it last. Deterministic, but two orders for one row. The price of H for rows: 1.45x of B in the activity kernel (comp), median +42 us per sweep, 7.79 ms against 6.29 ms over the 32, round regret 1.361 against 1.094.

Where the layout and count gains in cuOpt's scheme come from. C/P/A against C/P/R is 0.706 / 0.842; C/S/A against C/P/A is 0.9965 / 0.9992. The whole gain of 'S + A' over C/P/R (0.7035 / 0.8414) is the dropped count reduction; split arrays add nothing measurable once it is gone. With the split layout the extra integer reduction still costs 12% plain and 2% comp (C/S A / R 0.883 / 0.977).

Launch overhead bounds: one launch plus synchronise 9.0 us, each further launch about 3.2 us (37.9 us for ten). A B round has 2 to 8 launches, so at most about 31 us of the 61 to 95 us that a round costs in band A1 is launch and synchronise; the rest is thread latency and per-row work.

No longest-row rule rescues T. 'T when the longest row has at most 128 entries' gives a regret of 1.161 (worst 2.01 uccase9) against 1.094 for always B: T wins on kasavu, kenana, cygnet, supportcase42, sorrell3 but loses 1.3x to 7x on the small matrices with the same property (istanbul-no-cutoff 2.0x, uccase9 3.05x, piperout-d27 2.5x).

Plain arithmetic: the recommended B/S/A + B/S is not the best fixed combination; B/P/A + B/P has regret 1.121 against 1.136 (within 3% on 17 against 13 matrices), because the split layout costs 2.7% in the plain candidate kernel (P faster on 10 matrices, istanbul-no-cutoff 10.1%). The difference is inside the null band.

Warm numbers on an idle H200 with buffers allocated; the kernels that follow a round in a presolve (compaction of changed bounds, apply) are not included; nothing below 71,477 or above 2.7e7 nonzeros was measured.

analyst_open_questions: Bin boundary 64 with compensated sums: a 256-thread block costs about 23 ns per row in comp against 10 ns in plain, and on neos-5052403-cygnet (all rows 65 to 128 entries) one thread per row beats one block per row (0.670 ms against 0.877 ms). Would lane groups or one thread up to 128 or 256 entries be faster? Not measured.

Long columns in the candidate kernel: a block thread walks up to 32 entries at about 3 us each, and neos-4306827-ravan pays about 0.3 ms for 26 columns. Would a shorter block or chunk length (for example 1024 or 2048 entries) remove this? Not measured.

Scheme B runs its lane-group, block, chunk and finalize kernels one after another, and C beats it by up to 23% on matrices with few long rows (sp98ar, supportcase19, supportcase7, trento1). Would merging the classes into one launch, or overlapping launches, recover that?

Why is the compensated B candidate kernel 2.8% faster than the plain one (outside the spread on 19 matrices)? A rerun with the order of plain and comp swapped would tell whether it is the order of the run or code generation.

The column rule 'H when columns >= 1e5' is in-sample. Does it hold on the 8 large testbed instances without a sweep file (usafa, a2864-99blp, neos-3740487-motru, t11nonreg, neos-4332810-sesia, dlr2, hawaiiv10-130, neos-4535459-waipa) and on the held-out set?

What do B kernels cost on a frontier, with a state stored in binned order (no scattered write through the row map), and what does re-binning cost at a rebuild? The benchmark has a frontier kernel only for H/S/A, no frontier-restricted candidate kernel, and builds the bins on the host before timing.

Does the design need GPU activities that are bitwise equal to the host engine's one-thread sums? With B, hi and lo differ in bits from the one-thread result on 9 of 32 matrices (hi + lo is equal on all 32); only one thread per row (T, and H up to 64 entries) reproduces the bits.

All sweeps start from the original bounds and are one run per matrix on one idle H200. How do the count method and the gated lo load behave after tightening (fewer infinite terms, more rows with a nonzero lo), on a second GPU type, and with other work on the GPU?

engine.verified_summary:
Every number in the analyst's tables reproduces from the raw files. What needs correcting is three overstated statements and the weight put on modelled thresholds.

Full sweep. Measured: on all 32 matrices (71,477 to 27.3M nonzeros) the GPU round is cheaper than one CPU thread, 3.4x to 60x in plain arithmetic and 4.5x to 88x compensated against a CPU built with FMA; the kernel pair of DESIGN.md 2.4 is at least 2.6x faster (median 10x). In band A a host sweep costs 530 to 3,102 us and a GPU round 61 to 268 us. The crossover is below the measured range and extrapolated: 3,235 to 21,960 nonzeros from the fits, 8,954 to 55,553 per matrix with the designed pair (median 18,453). It is not true that it is never at 50,000: on a matrix like supportcase42, where most rows have two or more infinite terms and the host sweep costs 2.4 ns per nonzero, the two engines tie at 50,000 to 56,000.

Frontier. Measured on both sides for activities only: a GPU step costs 56 to 141 us on the smallest frontier (median 82); the cold host crosses it at a median of 9,940 frontier nonzeros (1,026 to 80,812), the warm host at 23,866. Everything about a whole step is modelled, because no frontier-restricted candidate kernel exists. (1) moves the crossover down, (2) and (3) move it up. None of the three is measured.

analyst_recommendations.evidence: All 32 measured matrices (71,477 nnz and above): GPU 3.4x to 88x faster. Fitted crossovers 3,235 to 21,960 nnz; per-matrix implied crossovers 4,194 to 35,950 (one matrix above 32,000: supportcase42, where the CPU by-row candidate pass has almost nothing to do); with the designed kernel pair 10,540 to 16,902; with a pageable upload of the matrix added 24,228.
analyst_recommendations.uncertainty: Extrapolated: no matrix below 71,477 nnz was measured, so 32,000 is 2.2x below the range. It does not bind anywhere in the target range. The 'best' round variant differs between matrices; the fixed designed pair is 1.31x slower in the median. It loses to the host only if the matrix first has to be uploaded from pageable memory on a matrix like supportcase42 (speedup 0.87). Re-measure with matrices of 20,000 to 70,000 nnz and the real kernels.

analyst_recommendations.decision: Frontier threshold (host below, GPU from it on), also used when the host owns the state
analyst_recommendations.value: W = frontier nonzeros + 8 x frontier rows >= 20,000 work units. If the work unit must stay plain nonzeros: 8,000 frontier nonzeros.
analyst_recommendations.evidence: Smallest summed loss over the 32 matrices at W = 11,314 (cold) to 26,909 (warm); with the host owning the state 13,454 (cold) and 22,627 (warm). W = 20,000 is within 1.01 to 1.27 of the best in the six scenarios A / S / H, cold and warm; T = 8,000 within 1.04 to 1.23. The row term cuts the spread of the per-matrix crossover from a factor 78.8 to 16.5 (activities, cold) and the worst factor at the threshold from 5.06 / 4.92 / 12.4 to 3.00 / 3.12 / 6.09.
analyst_recommendations.uncertainty: Wrong engine at the threshold costs up to 145 us per round for activities (measured on both sides; supportcase19) and up to 629 us for a step (supportcase19, host kept too long) or 365 us (supportcase7, GPU too early). The step numbers rest on a model (GPU step = 2 x its activity step) because no frontier-restricted candidate kernel exists; the measured bounds put the median crossover between 2,536 and 8,803 nonzeros. Cold and warm host costs differ by a factor 2.4 in the best threshold; 20,000 sits between them. Frontier lists were random rows. One GPU and one CPU only, so 'machine-independent' means calibrated on this pair. The CPU is assumed to be built with FMA; without it the compensated host sweep costs about 1.4x more and the threshold should drop.

analyst_recommendations.decision: Return threshold when the device owns the state (hysteresis)
analyst_recommendations.value: Host only below W = 8,000 if it has a mirror, below W = 4,000 if the rows must be gathered; otherwise the frontier stays on the GPU.
analyst_recommendations.evidence: Device owns the state, host cold plus dirty lists: smallest summed loss at W = 6,727 (within 10% from 4,757 to 9,514), median crossover 4,767 nonzeros; with the row gather added W = 4,000 (841 to 4,757), median 1,755, and below 30 nonzeros on three matrices. Hand-over costs: dirty list to the host 33 us, to the device 13 to 19 us, gather plus upload 61 us, against a GPU step floor of 56 to 141 us.
analyst_recommendations.uncertainty: One step only: if the host keeps the frontier for several rounds the hand-over is paid once and the threshold moves up towards 20,000; the number of host rounds per hand-over is not measured. Record counts are assumptions (one per frontier nonzero down, one per frontier row up). Built on the modelled GPU step. Using W = 20,000 here instead costs 1.85x (mirror) and 3.10x (gather) of the best summed loss.

analyst_recommendations.decision: Mirror size threshold on x86
analyst_recommendations.value: Pinned mirror while 12 bytes x nnz + 32 bytes x (rows + cols) <= 64 MiB (about 3.7M nonzeros at the testbed's median shape, 2.2M if the CSC is mirrored too); above it gather on demand.
analyst_recommendations.evidence: At 64 MiB a refresh costs 1,189 us = 19.5 gathers of up to 1,000 entries; 28 of the 32 matrices fit (not: neos-5116085-kenana, neos-5114902-kasavu, supportcase19, square47). In band A a refresh (31 to 184 us) equals 0.5 to 3 gathers and is 6% to 32% of the GPU rebuild it follows; in B3 14 to 30 gathers and 60% to 102% of the rebuild. Allocation of 64 MiB of pinned memory costs 18.2 ms once.
analyst_recommendations.uncertainty: Not derived from a measured break-even: the number of host row fetches between two rebuilds is unknown in Stage 0. The data only gives the exchange rate (T14): 16 MiB is right if there are about 5 fetches, 256 MiB if about 80. A rule that needs no size threshold in time terms is to gather on demand until the gathers since the last rebuild have cost one refresh and then refresh (my suggestion, not measured). Gather and dirty-list kernels are benchmark versions on a synthetic CSR with rows of 4 to 64 entries. The mirror must come from a warm pinned pool: allocating it inside the call costs 0.7 to 3.8 ms in band A (1.8% of HiGHS's time on supportcase40).

analyst_recommendations.decision: Device fixed-cost constants and budget in work units (1 unit = 10 ns, one host frontier nonzero; a frontier row = 8 units)
analyst_recommendations.value: Kernel launch in a chain 320; first launch + synchronisation 900; read-back 480 (1,380 on its own); library compaction (copy_if / select) 4,500; dirty list to the host 3,350; dirty list to the device 1,900; row gather with upload 6,100; measured floor of a frontier step 8,200 (median) to 14,100. Budget of device fixed cost per presolve call: 5 units (50 ns) per model nonzero.
analyst_recommendations.evidence: fixed_costs.json: 3.21 us per further launch, 9.01 us launch + sync, 4.83 us read-back, 44.5 us copy_if, 33.5 us and 19.0 us dirty lists, 60.8 us gather; sweeps: smallest frontier step 81.9 us median, 141 us maximum. The fitted cold host step costs 8.41 ns per nonzero and 88.3 ns per row. Budget: 50 ns per nonzero is 10% of HiGHS's smallest presolve time per nonzero (499 ns, supportcase42), 6.3% on supportcase40 and 1.75% in the median; it allows 37 / 31 / 23 round fixed costs (k = 4 / 8 / 16) at 50,000 nonzeros and 73 / 61 / 46 at 100,000.
analyst_recommendations.uncertainty: The 10% share is a policy choice, not a measurement. The launch model (64 to 119 us per round with one compaction) underestimates some measured steps (56 to 141 us): kernels with one thread per row are bound by thread latency, which a launch count does not capture. Thrust with cudaMalloc temporaries costs 289 us per call instead of 41, so the constants hold only with a pool. All constants are from one H200 and must be re-measured on a second GPU type before they are called machine-independent.

analyst_recommendations.decision: GPU: frontier list or all rows
analyst_recommendations.value: Sweep all rows without compaction on matrices up to 500,000 nonzeros; above that use the frontier list while it holds less than half of the nonzeros.
analyst_recommendations.evidence: At 10% of the rows the list is slower than the all-rows kernel on all 16 band A matrices and on 18 of 32; the rule 'list only above 500,000 nonzeros' picks the slower variant in 29 of 128 measured cases (1,079 us in total) against 41 cases (1,158 us) for 'always the list' and 87 cases (16,225 us) for 'always all rows'. Rules on the share of nonzeros alone lose 2,745 to 6,725 us.
analyst_recommendations.uncertainty: The gain over 'always the list' is small (at most 58 us per sweep). The 50% share is not measured: frontiers between 10% and 100% of the rows are missing, so the 'set fraction' of DESIGN.md 2.4 cannot be fixed from Stage 0. Applies to the activity kernel only.

analyst_recommendations.decision: Rebuild engine threshold (extra, DESIGN.md 2.3)
analyst_recommendations.value: Rebuild on the host below 100,000 matrix nonzeros, on the GPU from there on.
analyst_recommendations.evidence: GPU compact CSR + radix sort has a fixed part of 467 us and is slower than one CPU thread on the five matrices with 71,477 to 100,933 nonzeros except radiationm18-12-05 (0.56x to 0.985x); fitted crossover 86,442 (all 32) and 96,624 (band A). Measured inside the range.
analyst_recommendations.uncertainty: On the same sizes radiationm18-12-05 and supportcase40 already favour the GPU (1.38x, 1.06x), so the crossover depends on the structure. 20% deletions in every run; other deletion shares not measured. A host rebuild needs the matrix on the host (mirror) and a re-upload, which is not in the comparison. This section overlaps with the kernel analysis of another agent (stage0_kernels.py); I did not compare the two.

analyst_recommendations.decision: What Stage 1 must re-measure with the real kernels
analyst_recommendations.value: (1) A frontier-restricted candidate kernel on the device and the whole GPU step. (2) The real host engine per frontier nonzero and row: incremental activities, real frontiers, and cold after an actual device-to-host copy. (3) Launches, synchronisations and compactions per round of the real kernels, and the step floor. (4) Dirty-list sizes per hand-over and a flag-scan list on a model-sized state array. (5) Host row fetches between two rebuilds. (6) Full sweep and rebuild on matrices of 20,000 to 70,000 nonzeros. (7) The same tables on a second GPU type and a second CPU, with the CPU load recorded. (8) Frontiers between 10% and 100% of the rows on the GPU. (9) Row gather on the binned layout.
analyst_recommendations.evidence: Each item is a gap named in the findings: no device candidate kernel for frontiers (README_sweeps.md, Limits); benchmark versions of the dirty-list and gather kernels (README_fixed_costs.md, Limits); host-side timings disturbed by load (fixed_costs.json system); smallest matrix 71,477 nonzeros; one GPU and one CPU.
analyst_recommendations.uncertainty: Until then the frontier, return and mirror thresholds are provisional; only the full-sweep result (GPU cheaper on every matrix of 71,477 nonzeros and above) and the rebuild crossover are measured directly.

analyst_open_questions: Will the host engine be compiled with FMA? The CPU reference flags are -march=nocona, and without -mfma the compensated host sweep costs 10.7 instead of 7.6 ns per nonzero (std::fma is a libm call). All frontier crossovers above assume the FMA build; without it they drop and the threshold should be lower.

Is a row-weighted work unit (W = nonzeros + 8 x rows) acceptable for the work estimate of DESIGN.md 2.1, or must it stay plain nonzeros? Plain nonzeros cost about the same summed loss but a worst factor of 5 to 12 instead of 3 to 6 at the threshold.

One frontier threshold or two? The data supports a hysteresis by owner of the state on x86 (to the GPU at W >= 20,000; back to the host only below 8,000 with a mirror or 4,000 without). The plan names a single threshold.
How many times does a host phase fetch rows between two rebuilds? This decides the mirror threshold and Stage 0 has no data on it (16 MiB if about 5, 64 MiB if about 20, 256 MiB if about 80).
Does the host mirror need the CSC as well as the CSR? With both, 64 MiB corresponds to 2.2M instead of 3.7M nonzeros and only 24 of the 32 matrices fit.

How should the GPU compute candidates for a frontier: by row with an integer or min atomic into the columns, or by column over the columns the frontier touches? The cost of that kernel is the largest unknown in the step crossover (median between 2,536 and 8,803 frontier nonzeros).

Were the CPU times of the sweep files taken on an idle host? fixed_costs.json recorded a load average of 6.55 at its start; the sweep files have no such field, and warm times above cold times at the 10% frontier on several matrices (for example bab6, splice1k1) suggest some disturbance.

The 'set fraction' of DESIGN.md 2.4 (all rows instead of a frontier list) cannot be fixed from Stage 0: frontiers between 10% and 100% of the rows were not measured, and in band A the all-rows kernel is already as cheap as the list at 1% to 10%.
